r523: God designed the body to protect us in danger, and freezing is part of that protection, not a failure. Once the threat passes, slow breathing and movement tell the nervous system it is safe again. God also designed the thinking brain to weigh words. When Joseph wrote down what was said and separated fact from insult, he engaged his prefrontal cortex, which helps quieten the alarm. Speaking truth about himself, based on God's word, began laying down new pathways that slowly weakened the old shame story.
r524: Proverbs 15:1|A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger.
r528: The private meeting was awkward. His manager was defensive but stopped shouting at Joseph in meetings. Joseph improved his numbers over two quarters. When the manager later humiliated a colleague, Joseph helped her write to HR, and the manager received a formal warning. Joseph still flinches when voices are raised, but he no longer believes he is a joke.
r529: Harsh words describe the speaker's anger, not your worth, so you can calm down, learn what is true and respond with dignity.
r530: When a grown-up shouts mean words at you, those words are not who you are. God says you are precious.
r531: From Fear at Home to Safety
r532: Sunita, 36, mother of one in Delhi, in a verbally and emotionally abusive marriage
r533: Sunita has been married to Vikram for twelve years. In public he is charming. At home he calls her stupid, mocks her family, checks her phone, controls all the money and says no one else would ever want her. When she cries, he says she is too sensitive. Twice he threw things near her, and once he pushed her against a wall. Some church friends told her to pray more and submit. Sunita believed leaving would be a sin and would shame her parents. She became anxious, jumpy and unable to make even small decisions. One night, after Vikram threatened her in front of their daughter, Sunita finally called her sister and whispered, "I am scared."
r534: Ongoing verbal and emotional abuse keeps the nervous system on constant alert. Research suggests that living with chronic fear can affect memory, sleep, concentration and decision-making, which is why Sunita struggled with small choices. Abusers often isolate, confuse and blame, a pattern sometimes called coercive control. Over time the victim may come to doubt her own perception. Sunita also carried beliefs that kept her trapped, that suffering in silence was holy and that her worth depended on keeping the family together. The pushing and threats showed the danger was rising, which is a serious warning sign.
r535: Her sister helped her contact a women's helpline and a counsellor trained in abuse. For the first time someone told her clearly, "This is abuse. It is not your fault. God does not want you to live in danger." Sunita began planning for safety.
r536: Make a safety plan with a trained helpline or counsellor
r537: Keep documents, some money and key phone numbers somewhere safe
r538: Tell trusted family or friends what is happening
r539: Get legal help about protection orders and her rights
r540: Move to a safe place with her daughter when it is safe to go
r541: Get ongoing counselling and a safe church community for healing
r542: God sees the oppressed. Hagar, mistreated and alone, called Him "Thou God seest me" (Genesis 16:13). David fled from Saul when Saul tried to harm him, and God did not command him to stay (1 Samuel 19:10). Scripture tells husbands, "love your wives, and be not bitter against them" (Colossians 3:19), and to love "even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it" (Ephesians 5:25). Abuse breaks that covenant of love. The LORD is "a refuge for the oppressed, a refuge in times of trouble" (Psalm 9:9). Seeking safety is not a lack of faith. It is wisdom, and God goes with us.
r543: God designed the alarm system to protect us from danger, and in an abusive home it is telling the truth. Fear is a signal to seek safety, not a flaw to pray away. God also designed us to heal in safe relationships. Once a person is physically safe, the nervous system can slowly settle, sleep returns and thinking clears. Over time, with counselling and support, the brain can form new pathways of trust and confidence. God's design for healing begins with safety.
r544: Psalm 9:9|The LORD also will be a refuge for the oppressed, a refuge in times of trouble.
r548: With help from a helpline and a lawyer, Sunita and her daughter moved to her sister's home. Vikram first pleaded, then threatened, and she obtained a protection order. The early months were hard, with nightmares, guilt and money worries. Some church members criticised her. But a new church family welcomed her. A year later Sunita works part-time, sleeps through the night and is slowly rediscovering who she is.
r549: God never asks anyone to stay in danger, and seeking safety and help is wise and faithful.
r550: If someone at home keeps hurting you with words or hands, it is not your fault, and it is right to tell a safe adult and get to safety.
r553: Riya, fifteen, lives in Kolkata. After a falling out with a former friend, a class group chat started posting edited photos of her with cruel captions. Someone made a fake account in her name. Comments called her ugly, fat and worthless. Riya stopped eating lunch at school and checked her phone hundreds of times a day to see what new posts had appeared. She stopped going to youth group because some of the bullies attended. At night she scrolled through the comments, crying quietly so her parents would not hear. She thought about deleting everything and disappearing. She told no one, because she felt ashamed and afraid her parents would take away her phone.
r554: For teenagers, peer acceptance can feel like survival, and studies suggest the teenage brain is especially sensitive to social rejection. Online bullying is hard to escape because it follows a young person home and into bed. Checking the phone over and over kept Riya's stress response switched on, and the brain's natural focus on threats made each cruel comment stick more than the kind ones. Shame and fear kept her silent, which is very common, and bullies often rely on that silence. Riya also began to believe the words, because repeated messages, even false ones, can shape how we see ourselves.
r555: Her youth leader noticed she seemed withdrawn and gently asked. Riya broke down and told her everything. The leader helped her tell her parents, who responded with love, not punishment. For the first time, Riya felt she was not alone.
r556: Tell a trusted adult right away and save screenshots
r557: Report and block the accounts and the fake profile
r558: Involve the school and, if needed, the cyber crime police
r559: Keep the phone outside the bedroom at night
r560: Speak God's truth about herself out loud each morning
r561: Spend time with real friends who are kind
r562: Words can wound deeply. Proverbs says, "Death and life are in the power of the tongue" (Proverbs 18:21). But God's words about us are truer than any comment. David prayed, "I will praise thee, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made" (Psalm 139:14). Jesus was mocked and lied about, yet He knew who He was and whose He was. God promises, "Fear thou not, for I am with thee... I will strengthen thee" (Isaiah 41:10). When lies multiply, Scripture tells us to think on "whatsoever things are true" (Philippians 4:8). Our value comes from the God who made us and loves us.
r563: God made the brain able to change. When cruel words are repeated, they can carve a path, but true words repeated can carve new ones. Speaking truth out loud uses hearing, speech and memory together, which may help it stick more strongly. God also designed us for safe connection. When Riya told safe adults, her stress began to settle because she was no longer carrying the burden alone. Keeping the phone away at night also let sleep restore her brain and mood.
r564: Psalm 139:14|I will praise thee, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works.
r568: The school identified two students behind the fake account, and they were suspended. The posts came down. Riya still felt anxious for months and sometimes cried when she saw old photos. She met a school counsellor regularly and slowly returned to youth group, where a few new friends welcomed her. Her family now keeps all phones out of bedrooms at night.
r569: Bullying grows in silence, so telling a safe adult and speaking God's truth over yourself breaks its power.
r570: If people are mean to you online, tell a grown-up you trust right away. You are not alone, and God says you are wonderful.
r571: The Volunteer Who Could Not Say No
r572: Benny, 41, IT professional and church volunteer in Bengaluru
r573: Benny Mathew is the person everyone at his Bengaluru church calls when something needs doing. He runs the sound system, drives elderly members to services, leads a home group, organises the Christmas programme and fixes the pastor's laptop. He also works full time in IT. When asked to help, he says yes before he thinks. Recently he started feeling exhausted, irritable and secretly angry at people who ask him for things. He missed his daughter's school concert because of a church meeting, and she cried. One Sunday he sat in the car park unable to walk in. He felt guilty for even wanting to say no. "If I don't do it, who will?" he kept asking himself.
r574: People-pleasing often grows from early learning. Benny grew up with a father who drank and a mother who was often overwhelmed. As a boy, being helpful kept the peace and earned praise. His nervous system learned that being useful was the way to be safe and loved. So now, when someone asks, his brain predicts rejection or conflict if he says no, and the yes comes out automatically. Research suggests that chronic overcommitment without rest can lead to burnout, with exhaustion, cynicism and lower effectiveness. His secret resentment was a signal that his own needs had been ignored for too long.
r575: His wife sat with him and asked, "Who are you afraid will stop loving you if you say no?" Benny realised it was not God. He began learning that a godly no can protect a better yes.
r576: Pause before every request and say, let me pray and check
r577: Name the fear behind each automatic yes
r578: List his real needs for sleep, family and rest
r579: Step down from two roles and train others to take them
r580: Treat resentment as a signal to set a boundary
r581: Keep one evening a week only for family
r582: Even Jesus said no. When the crowds were searching for Him, He said, "Let us go into the next towns, that I may preach there also, for therefore came I forth" (Mark 1:38). He often "withdrew himself into the wilderness, and prayed" (Luke 5:16). Moses tried to do everything until his father-in-law Jethro said, "The thing that thou doest is not good... thou art not able to perform it thyself alone" (Exodus 18:17-18). Paul wrote that each person should give "not grudgingly, or of necessity, for God loveth a cheerful giver" (2 Corinthians 9:7). Service from fear is not the same as service from love.
r583: God designed us with limits. We need sleep, food, rest and relationships, and the Sabbath was built into creation as a gift. When we ignore these limits, the body raises warning signs like fatigue, irritability and resentment. These signals are not sinful. They are God-given alarms. God also made the brain able to learn new responses. Each time Benny paused and chose a thoughtful answer instead of an automatic yes, he strengthened a new pathway, making healthy choices easier over time.
r584: Mark 6:31|Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while.
r588: Some people were disappointed, and one leader said Benny was becoming less committed. That hurt. But the sound team found two new volunteers who loved the work. Benny attended every one of his daughter's events that term. He still slips into automatic yeses when he is tired, but he catches himself faster now. He says he enjoys serving again.
r589: A loving no, said without fear, protects the yes God has really asked of you.
r590: It is okay to say no sometimes. God loves you because you are His, not because you do everything.
r591: The Eldest Daughter Who Gave Everything
r592: Sneha, 31, eldest of four siblings in Nagpur
r593: Sneha is thirty-one and the eldest of four children in Nagpur. When she was twelve, her father fell ill, and she began cooking, caring for her siblings and helping in the family shop. Later she paid for her brother's engineering degree and her sister's wedding. She turned down a job in Pune and a marriage proposal because her mother said the family needed her. Now her siblings are settled, but they still call her for money and problems. Sneha feels tired, lonely and invisible. When she buys something for herself, she feels guilty. When she thinks of saying no, her chest tightens with fear. "If I stop giving, will anyone still love me?" she wrote in her journal.
r594: When a child takes on adult responsibilities too early, psychologists call it parentification. Sneha's growing brain learned that her value lay in being needed, and that her own wants were selfish. Her nervous system linked saying no with danger, the fear of being abandoned or blamed. This is part of the fawn response, where we try to stay safe by pleasing others. Cultural expectations of eldest daughters reinforced it. Over years, constant self-sacrifice without care can lead to exhaustion, hidden resentment and loss of identity. Her guilt was not a sign of sin, but of an old rule that needed updating.
r595: At a women's retreat, a speaker said, "Jesus told us to love our neighbour as ourselves, not instead of ourselves." Sneha wept. She began to see that caring for herself was not selfish, but part of stewarding the life God gave her.
r596: Write down the fear behind each yes to her family
r597: Make a list of her own needs and dreams
r598: Say no to one request a week, kindly and clearly
r599: Ask her siblings to share family responsibilities
r600: See a Christian counsellor to grieve her lost childhood
